title: If You've Saved This Much, You're Ahead of Almost Every Retiree
description:
How much do you actually need to be in the top 1% of retirees? Discover why a $200,000 balance puts you ahead of most Americans—and why it still might not be enough.

This video breaks down the actual retirement savings percentiles for American households, revealing that a $1 million balance puts you in the top 3.2% of all retirees. We analyze Federal Reserve data and Vanguard reports to show why the median balance of $200,000 for those aged 65-74 is misleading once you account for the 40% of adults with zero savings. Beyond the "pile of money," we explore the 4% rule and how safe withdrawal rates translate into monthly checks compared to the average Social Security benefit of $2,084. We also address the looming $185,500 per-person healthcare bill and why 46% of workers are forced into early retirement due to health issues or downsizing. Learn why the "retirement savings puzzle" keeps even wealthy retirees from spending their money and how new Secure 2.0 "super catch-up" rules can add $140,000 to your balance in just four years. Finally, we examine why the structure of your guaranteed income matters more than your percentile ranking when it comes to long-term financial security.

title: I'm 62 ... If You Are In Your 40s or 50s, Watch This
description:
Retirement planning isn’t just about reaching a "number"—it’s about protecting your final 900 Saturdays from the risks no one tells you about. A former financial advisor reveals why 46% of people retire earlier than planned and how to bridge the gap between your portfolio and reality.

After 20 years as a financial advisor, I’ve seen the "Am I going to be okay?" question answered with the wrong data. Most people plan for a retirement date they won’t actually choose, as layoffs, health issues, or family caregiving duties often force an exit years earlier than expected. This video breaks down the "active years" math—the limited Saturdays you have left—and why your real spending won't follow a straight line. We explore the massive impact of involuntary retirement on Social Security benefits, the hidden $1 trillion cost of caregiving, and why comparing your savings to the "average" balance is a dangerous mistake. You'll learn how to build a portfolio that survives a bear market without selling at the bottom and why an "80% success" probability is often better than trading your healthiest years for 97% certainty. Finally, we look at the specific 401(k) catch-up window between ages 60 and 63 that many savers miss and why the trips you postpone are the ones that eventually expire.

title: The Paycheck Gap Between $500K and $800K in Retirement
description:
Does a $300,000 gap in retirement savings actually buy a different lifestyle, or just a different set of tax problems? The math between $500,000 and $800,000 reveals why the balance on your statement is often the weakest number in your plan.

This breakdown compares two realistic retirement scenarios to see how much "extra" life a larger portfolio actually provides in today's economy. While $800,000 generates more raw income, we analyze how Social Security compression, 1984 tax thresholds, and Medicare surcharges narrow the gap between "comfortable" and "constrained." Using specific withdrawal data from Morningstar and 4% rule creator Bill Bengen, the video explores the "tax torpedo" of provisional income and the urgent "scheduling problem" created by Required Minimum Distributions (RMDs) at age 73. We also examine the 2025 CareScout cost of care survey to show why a larger balance serves less as a luxury upgrade and more as "reserve capacity" for a $115,000-a-year nursing home stay. Finally, you will see why eliminating a $1,000 monthly mortgage is mathematically identical to adding $300,000 to your 401(k), proving that what you spend matters more than what you save.

title: Vanguard Says YOU Are Holding Too Much Cash
description:
Most retirement advice tells you to keep 1 to 3 years of cash, but that "safety" might be costing you a fortune. New data suggests the way you calculate your cash buffer could be the difference between a portfolio that lasts and one that runs dry.

You will learn why sizing your "survivor gap" is more critical than your joint gap and how sequence of returns risk changes when your floor is guaranteed. We examine the "two-legged" retirement structure: Social Security as your indexed income leg and your portfolio as the leg that must manufacture its own raises. By analyzing a hypothetical market correction and the opportunity cost of holding too much cash, we identify why a 30-50% equity allocation is often the mathematical peak for safe withdrawal rates. You will learn how to calculate your indexed share ratio to determine if your retirement plan is structurally capable of covering the rising cost of living. Ultimately, the goal is to transition from an accumulation mindset to a production mindset to ensure your paycheck keeps up with the Bureau of Labor Statistics' actual cost of aging.

title: Once Your Income Hits This Number, Medicare Costs Jump
description:

We examine the specific definition of Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI) that Medicare uses, including the surprising inclusion of tax-exempt municipal bond interest. By analyzing the "2-year look-back" mechanism, we explain why retirees often receive bill increases for decisions made years ago that cannot be appealed through Form SSA-44. Discover why the habit of tax deferral can actually work against you in retirement and how to transition from "maximizing a balance" to "scheduling income" to protect your portfolio from unbudgeted surcharges.

description:

We also debunk the infamous Boeing actuarial chart and reveal why the real risk for most retirees isn't dying too soon, but outliving their assets. For a healthy couple, there is a 60% chance at least one spouse lives into their 90s, requiring a joint runway that accounts for sequence of returns risk, Social Security timing, and surviving spouse tax brackets.

Crossing the "permission line" in retirement isn't just about the math; it's about shifting from a saver to a spender without the guilt. If your portfolio is 25x your annual needs, the barrier to freedom is likely psychological, not financial.

This video explores the "retirement savings puzzle"—the phenomenon where retirees with substantial assets often refuse to spend them, even when the math suggests they are safe. We break down the 25x rule of thumb and why a $1 million portfolio supporting a $40,000 annual gap serves as a conservative "permission line" for many. You’ll learn about the original William Bengen 4% rule research and how later asset class expansions actually increased the safe withdrawal max to roughly 4.7%. We conduct a "fear audit" on unpriced risks like longevity, Social Security depletion projections for 2032, and the $130,000 annual reality of long-term care. By assigning specific jobs to your assets—separating contingency funds from legacy goals—you can stop making your daily budget compete with catastrophe. Finally, the video provides a framework for turning a volatile portfolio into a "retirement paycheck" to separate daily spending decisions from lifetime solvency.

title: Social Security at 62 vs 70: The Math Everyone Gets Wrong
description:
Is claiming Social Security at 62 or 70 better for your portfolio? The real break-even age isn't a fixed point at 82 once you account for real investment returns and sequence of returns risk.

Deciding when to claim Social Security involves a high-stakes trade-off between near-term liquidity and a permanent, inflation-adjusted income floor. While a basic comparison of a $3,000 primary insurance amount suggests a crossover at age 80, factoring in a modest 4% real return on preserved assets can push that date past age 86. This analysis breaks down how delaying benefits creates a massive "bridge load," potentially forcing a dangerous 9% initial withdrawal rate on a $500,000 portfolio. We examine how the 2032 trust fund projections, federal income tax rules, and Medicare IRMAA surcharges change the net value of your checks. The discussion also covers the critical role of survivor benefits for married couples and why path dependence makes smooth spreadsheet math unreliable in a volatile market. Ultimately, your personal health horizon and asset capacity determine if your portfolio can safely finance the route to age 70.

Social Security is giving retirees a 3.6% raise in January 2027. For a lot of couples on Medicare, a line on a tax return they already filed will take back more than that whole raise.

In this video we walk through the big Medicare changes for 2027, in dollars, for a real household:
